screens.title: Byte Streams: Working with Raw Data
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on byte streams — the tools Java provides to read and write raw bytes for images, audio, video, and compiled code. You will learn how FileInputStream and FileOutputStream move individual bytes to and from files, why naive byte-by-byte copying can be slow, and how buffering changes performance by batching system calls. We also cover decorator streams, specifically BufferedInputStream and BufferedOutputStream, show a robust pattern for copying files with try-with-resources, and point out common mistakes like forgetting to flush, accidentally overwriting files, and not handling FileNotFoundException. As an example, you'll see a buffered file copy that reads chunks into a byte array and writes the valid bytes out, measuring time to compare buffered versus unbuffered approaches. By the end you'll be able to pick the right stream for binary input and output, wrap streams to gain buffering, and write safe, efficient copy utilities. Why does this matter? Because efficient file input and output removes a common bottleneck in real applications that handle media or large datasets. Think of a photo upload feature: correct use of byte streams preserves file bytes and improves speed. What file will you copy first to test buffering?

Byte Streams: Working with Raw Data

Learn how Java reads and writes raw bytes, why buffering changes performance, and how to copy binary files reliably.

Quick visual
File bytes flow
Buffer batches
In this lesson
FileInputStream, FileOutputStream, buffering, try-with-resources, and safe copying patterns.
Coming up
Live coding: unbuffered copy then buffered refactor with timing comparison.
Why it matters
Efficient binary I/O prevents slow file operations and preserves exact bytes for media and compiled files.
Explore Key Topics
Byte streams
Use to read or write raw binary data like images and audio without character encoding.
Buffering
Batch I/O operations into memory to reduce expensive system calls and improve throughput.
Try-with-resources
Automatically closes streams to avoid resource leaks and make code robust.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives define the measurable skills you will leave this chapter with. First, you'll implement file read and write operations using FileInputStream and FileOutputStream so you can move raw bytes reliably between disk and your program. Second, you will understand buffering: why BufferedInputStream and BufferedOutputStream reduce system calls and speed up large file transfers. Third, you'll practice copying binary files and ensuring data integrity by reading into a buffer and writing only the valid bytes returned by read. Fourth, you'll apply try-with-resources to manage streams safely and learn to handle common exceptions like FileNotFoundException and general IOExceptions. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with a concrete coding task: read a small binary file, switch to buffered streams, measure time differences, and demonstrate correct use of try-with-resources. By the end you will not only know the A P I names but also understand trade-offs such as buffer size and overwriting versus appending. These are practical skills used whenever your app handles media files, binary protocols, or file-based caching. Keep these objectives in mind as checkpoints as you work through the code examples and hands-on activity.

screens.title: When to use byte streams
screens.narratorSegment: A byte stream transfers raw binary data between your program and a file or device. Use byte streams whenever you must preserve exact bytes — that includes images, audio files, video, compressed files, and compiled code. Unlike character streams, which interpret bytes using a charset and may translate or corrupt binary sequences, byte streams deliver each byte unchanged. A concrete example: when saving a JPEG image, using a character reader would try to decode bytes into characters and inevitably damage the file; FileInputStream lets you read the JPEG bytes exactly as they are. A common misconception is to prefer character streams for simplicity; that works when working with text files but fails for binary formats. Another mistake is assuming byte streams handle character encoding — they don't. If you need text, wrap a byte stream in a reader with a specified charset. Key takeaway: choose FileInputStream/FileOutputStream when data must remain byte-for-byte identical. Try asking yourself: is the file human-readable text? If not, prefer a byte stream to avoid accidental corruption. When to use byte streams means byte streams move raw bytes and are essential for binary formats because they preserve exact byte sequences.. In practical terms, why byte streams are the right tool for non-textual data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › When to use byte streams
Core Concept

When to use byte streams

Use byte streams for any non-textual data that must keep exact bytes intact.

  • • Definition: raw, unencoded bytes moved without character interpretation.
  • • Example: copying a JPEG or MP3 file exactly byte-for-byte preserves integrity.
  • • Contrast: character streams may change bytes due to charset conversion and are unsuitable for binary files.
Key Takeaway

If a file is not plain text, use a byte stream to avoid corruption from character encoding.

Analogy

Think of bytes as physical Lego pieces. Byte streams carry each piece without changing its shape. Character streams try to read those pieces as words, which breaks the model.

Quick checklist
Binary format? Yes
Preserve exact bytes
Do not use readers
Use try-with-resources

screens.title: FileInputStream: Reading bytes
screens.narratorSegment: FileInputStream reads bytes from a file and exposes them to your program as integers between zero and 255, or -1 to signal end-of-file. When you call the single-byte read method, it returns an int because Java needs a sentinel value for EOF. A more efficient pattern is to call a read method that fills a byte array and returns the number of bytes actually read; this reduces method call overhead. For example, reading into a 4KB buffer returns a count less than the buffer when near the file end. Be prepared to catch FileNotFoundException when constructing a FileInputStream — it indicates the file path is wrong or not accessible. A common misconception is to assume read always fills the buffer; it may return a smaller count, and you should use that count when writing or processing the buffer. In practice: open the stream in try-with-resources, loop until read returns -1, and on each iteration process only the valid range returned. This pattern both preserves data and avoids subtle bugs caused by leftover bytes in the buffer. In practical terms, how fileinputstream returns bytes and handles eof and errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › FileInputStream
Definition

FileInputStream reads raw bytes

It returns an int per read call, or fills a byte[] and returns a count of bytes read.

// Pattern: read into buffer and use returned count
int bytesRead;
byte[] buffer = new byte[4096];
try (java.io.FileInputStream fis = new java.io.FileInputStream("input.bin")) {
  while ((bytesRead = fis.read(buffer)) != -1) {
    // process buffer[0 .. bytesRead-1]
  }
} catch (java.io.IOException e) {
  // handle error
}
Practical notes
  • • Constructor may throw FileNotFoundException — verify paths and permissions.
  • • Read returns -1 at EOF; do not assume a full buffer on the final read.
  • • Prefer bulk reads into byte arrays to reduce method/system call overhead.
Common mistake

Using the buffer contents directly without checking the returned byte count can add garbage bytes to output or cause data corruption.

screens.title: FileOutputStream: Writing bytes and append vs overwrite
screens.narratorSegment: FileOutputStream writes raw bytes to a file. The write methods accept either a single int (which is cast to a byte) or a byte array; there are overloads that take an offset and length to write only part of an array. By default, creating a FileOutputStream with a file path truncates the file — it overwrites existing contents. If you want to add bytes to a file instead, use the constructor overload that accepts a boolean append flag set to true. A concrete scenario: logging binary diagnostics to the same file requires append; accidentally omitting append can silently erase previous logs. Another important point is to call flush when you need guaranteed immediate persistence of buffered data; otherwise BufferedOutputStream may hold data until its buffer is full or the stream is closed. A common misconception is that closing always flushes — while close usually flushes, relying on explicit flush before critical checkpoints avoids surprises. The safe pattern is: open streams with try-with-resources, write bytes using write(buffer, 0, len), optionally call flush when needed, and avoid accidental overwrites by checking file existence or using append when appropriate.

keyIdea.text: FileOutputStream overwrites by default; use the append constructor to add bytes and write byte arrays with offset and length to control output.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › FileOutputStream
Definition

FileOutputStream writes raw bytes

You can overwrite or append; use write(int) or write(byte[], offset, len) for controlled output.

// Overwrite mode (default)
try (java.io.FileOutputStream fos = new java.io.FileOutputStream("out.bin")) {
  fos.write(buffer, 0, bytesRead);
}

// Append mode
try (java.io.FileOutputStream fos = new java.io.FileOutputStream("out.bin", true)) {
  fos.write(buffer, 0, bytesRead);
}
Practical tips
  • • Check if overwriting is safe before opening the stream in default mode.
  • • Use append=true only when you intend to add bytes, like logs or incremental data.
  • • Call flush explicitly when you need buffered bytes written immediately.
Common mistake

Opening in overwrite mode without checking file existence can destroy data. Confirm your intent before writing.

screens.title: Naive file copy: byte-by-byte
screens.narratorSegment: A naive unbuffered copy reads a single byte from the source and writes it immediately to the destination in a tight loop. Functionally it works, and for tiny files the difference is invisible. But each read and write call typically triggers a system call to the operating system, which is expensive compared to memory operations. As file size grows, the cumulative overhead of millions of system calls slows your program dramatically. A concrete example: copying a 10 megabyte file byte-by-byte results in roughly 10 million read and write operations — a large number of system calls. This approach also places more pressure on C P U context switching and input and output scheduling. Contrast that with buffered copying, where a single system call moves a block of kilobytes into memory and subsequent loop iterations operate on that memory. Common misconceptions include believing modern OS caching eliminates the penalty; while OS caching helps, method call and syscall overhead remain significant. Key takeaway: prefer bulk reads into byte arrays rather than single-byte reads when copying files. Naive file copy: byte-by-byte means single-byte read/write causes many system calls; use bulk reads into a buffer to reduce overhead and improve throughput.. In practical terms, what happens when you copy one byte at a time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Naive file copy
Process Flow

Byte-by-byte copy

Read one byte and write it immediately in a loop. Correct but inefficient for larger files.

Steps
  1. Create FileInputStream and FileOutputStream.
  2. Call read() -> int; check for -1.
  3. Call write(int) for each byte read.
  4. Close streams (or use try-with-resources).
Concrete example

Copying a 5 MB image with one-byte operations causes millions of read/write calls and becomes noticeably slower than a buffered copy. The lesson is to reduce the number of system calls by reading blocks of bytes instead.

Contrast

System-level caching helps, but does not eliminate the overhead of repeated read/write calls and method dispatch in the JVM.

Key Takeaway

Prefer buffer-backed copying for any realistically sized file to avoid heavy syscall costs.

screens.title: Buffering: What it is and why it helps
screens.narratorSegment: Buffering stores data in memory temporarily so that your program can read and write in larger blocks instead of making many small system calls. When you wrap a FileInputStream with a BufferedInputStream, the wrapper performs an underlying read once to fill its internal buffer and then serves subsequent byte requests from memory. This reduces context switches and the number of expensive disk reads. A concrete example: a 4KB buffer causes roughly one system call per 4KB of file data, versus one per byte without buffering. BufferedOutputStream behaves similarly on writes: it collects bytes into an internal buffer and writes them out in larger chunks. A common misconception is that buffering only reduces latency; in fact, it primarily increases throughput by reducing syscall overhead. Another developer pitfall is choosing an extremely large buffer; while bigger buffers reduce syscalls further, they also use more memory and can yield diminishing returns. Start with 4KB to 8KB, measure performance, and adjust based on empirical results. The main takeaway: buffering moves work from slow input and output to fast memory operations. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Buffering
Core Concept

Buffering batches I/O

An internal buffer reduces the number of costly system calls by handling many bytes in memory at once.

  • A single underlying read fills the buffer, and subsequent reads use the buffer.
  • BufferedOutputStream accumulates bytes and issues fewer, larger writes.
  • Start with a 4KB–8KB buffer and tune with measurements.
Analogy & example

Think of a buffer as a delivery truck: instead of sending one envelope per trip, load many envelopes into the truck. For a 10MB file, a 4KB buffer reduces trips significantly compared to single-byte sends.

Pro tip

Measure with System.nanoTime before and after copying to quantify the improvement when you add buffering.

screens.title: Buffered file copy: code example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a buffered file copy pattern. The example wraps a FileInputStream in a BufferedInputStream and a FileOutputStream in a BufferedOutputStream inside a try-with-resources block. The loop reads into a byte[] buffer and returns bytesRead; the write call then writes buffer starting at zero for bytesRead length. This ensures the final partial buffer doesn't write unused bytes. The try-with-resources ensures both streams close automatically, preventing leaks even on exceptions. Notice the use of a 4096-byte buffer — a reasonable default that balances syscall reduction and memory usage. A common misconception is that BufferedOutputStream will always flush automatically; while close flushes, calling flush explicitly before critical points is good practice. For error handling, catch IOException to report problems such as FileNotFoundException from constructors. The concrete code shows how to measure elapsed time using nanoTime to compare buffered versus unbuffered versions. As a closing question: how would you change the buffer size to profile performance for larger or smaller files? content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Buffered file copy
Code Walkthrough

BufferedFileCopier pattern

try (java.io.BufferedInputStream bis = new java.io.BufferedInputStream(new java.io.FileInputStream(sourceFile));
     java.io.BufferedOutputStream bos = new java.io.BufferedOutputStream(new java.io.FileOutputStream(destFile))) {

  byte[] buffer = new byte[4096];
  int bytesRead;
  while ((bytesRead = bis.read(buffer)) != -1) {
    bos.write(buffer, 0, bytesRead);
  }
  bos.flush();
} catch (java.io.IOException e) {
  e.printStackTrace();
}
Explanation bullets
  • • Wrapping adds buffering without changing underlying stream semantics.
  • • Read returns number of bytes read; write uses that count to avoid writing stale buffer data.
  • • Try-with-resources closes both buffered and file streams reliably.
Key Takeaway

This buffered loop is the standard, efficient pattern for copying binary files in Java.

screens.title: Try-with-resources: safe and concise closing
screens.narratorSegment: Try-with-resources ensures streams are closed automatically when a block finishes or when an exception is thrown. For file streams, this prevents file descriptors being leaked, which could otherwise exhaust system resources in long-running processes. The pattern is simple: declare your streams in the try(...) header and omit explicit close calls. Under the hood, the JVM calls close on each AutoCloseable in reverse order, which also flushes BufferedOutputStream. Avoid the mistake of catching exceptions and swallowing them without ensuring closure. A concrete example: if a copy operation throws an IOException while writing, try-with-resources still closes the streams and flushes buffered output on close, reducing the risk of truncated files. If you need to guarantee data reaches disk immediately before continuing, call flush explicitly; close will usually flush, but flush before critical points is safer. Overall, prefer try-with-resources for clarity and resource safety in all stream-based input and output. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. screens.narratorSegment: This slide collects common errors you should guard against. First, forgetting to flush buffered output can leave recent writes in memory; while close normally flushes, call flush explicitly if you need immediate persistence before continuing. Second, not using try-with-resources or failing to close streams can leak file descriptors. Third, creating a FileOutputStream without checking can overwrite important data — use the append constructor or check file existence when appropriate. Fifth, choosing an inappropriate buffer size either wastes memory (too large) or reduces benefit (too small). screens.title: Comparing unbuffered vs buffered copies
screens.narratorSegment: After running both versions, interpreting the results helps you tune real code. Buffered copies usually show a large drop in elapsed time because they replace many small system calls with fewer, larger ones. Use System. nanoTime to measure start and end times and convert to milliseconds for readable output. Compare three runs to reduce variance and take the median. When experimenting with buffer sizes, you'll often see large gains moving from single-byte to 4KB, smaller additional gains up to 8KB, and diminishing returns beyond that on many systems. However, very large buffers may consume significant heap memory or interact poorly with the underlying filesystem block size; empirical testing on your target environment is essential. A misconception is to assume the largest buffer is always best — it isn't. Also, consider measuring wall-clock time under representative load and avoid microbenchmarks that do not reflect real-world disk behavior. The final takeaway: measurement drives tuning; use small controlled experiments to find the sweet spot for your workload. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on byte streams — the tools Java provides to read and write raw bytes for images, audio, video, and compiled code. You will learn how FileInputStream and FileOutputStream move individual bytes to and from files, why naive byte-by-byte copying can be slow, and how buffering changes performance by batching system calls. We also cover decorator streams, specifically BufferedInputStream and BufferedOutputStream, show a robust pattern for copying files with try-with-resources, and point out common mistakes like forgetting to flush, accidentally overwriting files, and not handling FileNotFoundException. As an example, you'll see a buffered file copy that reads chunks into a byte array and writes the valid bytes out, measuring time to compare buffered versus unbuffered approaches. By the end you'll be able to pick the right stream for binary input and output, wrap streams to gain buffering, and write safe, efficient copy utilities. Why does this matter? Because efficient file input and output removes a common bottleneck in real applications that handle media or large datasets. Think of a photo upload feature: correct use of byte streams preserves file bytes and improves speed. What file will you copy first to test buffering?

These objectives define the measurable skills you will leave this chapter with. First, you'll implement file read and write operations using FileInputStream and FileOutputStream so you can move raw bytes reliably between disk and your program. Second, you will understand buffering: why BufferedInputStream and BufferedOutputStream reduce system calls and speed up large file transfers. Third, you'll practice copying binary files and ensuring data integrity by reading into a buffer and writing only the valid bytes returned by read. Fourth, you'll apply try-with-resources to manage streams safely and learn to handle common exceptions like FileNotFoundException and general IOExceptions. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with a concrete coding task: read a small binary file, switch to buffered streams, measure time differences, and demonstrate correct use of try-with-resources. By the end you will not only know the A P I names but also understand trade-offs such as buffer size and overwriting versus appending. These are practical skills used whenever your app handles media files, binary protocols, or file-based caching. Keep these objectives in mind as checkpoints as you work through the code examples and hands-on activity.

You will show understanding through a small hands-on comparison and a short reflective task. First, implement an unbuffered copy using FileInputStream and FileOutputStream to see the baseline performance. Then refactor the same code to use BufferedInputStream and BufferedOutputStream with a 4KB or 8KB buffer, measure the time, and compare results. This practical exercise enforces the conceptual point that buffering reduces system calls and improves throughput. You will also use try-with-resources in both versions; that demonstrates safe closing of streams even when exceptions occur. Finally, document one scenario where overwriting a file is dangerous and explain how you would prevent it in code. These actions test both coding skill and judgment about when to append, when to overwrite, and how to handle FileNotFoundException. The assessment encourages experimentation: try different buffer sizes and watch how the elapsed time changes. Record a short note about what you observed and whether larger buffers improved or plateaued performance for your sample file.

A byte stream transfers raw binary data between your program and a file or device. Use byte streams whenever you must preserve exact bytes — that includes images, audio files, video, compressed files, and compiled code. Unlike character streams, which interpret bytes using a charset and may translate or corrupt binary sequences, byte streams deliver each byte unchanged. A concrete example: when saving a JPEG image, using a character reader would try to decode bytes into characters and inevitably damage the file; FileInputStream lets you read the JPEG bytes exactly as they are. A common misconception is to prefer character streams for simplicity; that works when working with text files but fails for binary formats. Another mistake is assuming byte streams handle character encoding — they don't. If you need text, wrap a byte stream in a reader with a specified charset. Key takeaway: choose FileInputStream/FileOutputStream when data must remain byte-for-byte identical. Try asking yourself: is the file human-readable text? If not, prefer a byte stream to avoid accidental corruption. When to use byte streams means byte streams move raw bytes and are essential for binary formats because they preserve exact byte sequences.. In practical terms, why byte streams are the right tool for non-textual data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

FileInputStream reads bytes from a file and exposes them to your program as integers between zero and 255, or -1 to signal end-of-file. When you call the single-byte read method, it returns an int because Java needs a sentinel value for EOF. A more efficient pattern is to call a read method that fills a byte array and returns the number of bytes actually read; this reduces method call overhead. For example, reading into a 4KB buffer returns a count less than the buffer when near the file end. Be prepared to catch FileNotFoundException when constructing a FileInputStream — it indicates the file path is wrong or not accessible. A common misconception is to assume read always fills the buffer; it may return a smaller count, and you should use that count when writing or processing the buffer. In practice: open the stream in try-with-resources, loop until read returns -1, and on each iteration process only the valid range returned. This pattern both preserves data and avoids subtle bugs caused by leftover bytes in the buffer. FileInputStream: Reading bytes means use read(byte[]) and the returned count; check for -1 to detect end-of-file and handle filenotfoundexception on construction.. In practical terms, how fileinputstream returns bytes and handles eof and errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

FileOutputStream writes raw bytes to a file. The write methods accept either a single int (which is cast to a byte) or a byte array; there are overloads that take an offset and length to write only part of an array. By default, creating a FileOutputStream with a file path truncates the file — it overwrites existing contents. If you want to add bytes to a file instead, use the constructor overload that accepts a boolean append flag set to true. A concrete scenario: logging binary diagnostics to the same file requires append; accidentally omitting append can silently erase previous logs. Another important point is to call flush when you need guaranteed immediate persistence of buffered data; otherwise BufferedOutputStream may hold data until its buffer is full or the stream is closed. A common misconception is that closing always flushes — while close usually flushes, relying on explicit flush before critical checkpoints avoids surprises. The safe pattern is: open streams with try-with-resources, write bytes using write(buffer, 0, len), optionally call flush when needed, and avoid accidental overwrites by checking file existence or using append when appropriate.

A naive unbuffered copy reads a single byte from the source and writes it immediately to the destination in a tight loop. Functionally it works, and for tiny files the difference is invisible. But each read and write call typically triggers a system call to the operating system, which is expensive compared to memory operations. As file size grows, the cumulative overhead of millions of system calls slows your program dramatically. A concrete example: copying a 10 megabyte file byte-by-byte results in roughly 10 million read and write operations — a large number of system calls. This approach also places more pressure on C P U context switching and input and output scheduling. Contrast that with buffered copying, where a single system call moves a block of kilobytes into memory and subsequent loop iterations operate on that memory. Common misconceptions include believing modern OS caching eliminates the penalty; while OS caching helps, method call and syscall overhead remain significant. Key takeaway: prefer bulk reads into byte arrays rather than single-byte reads when copying files. Naive file copy: byte-by-byte means single-byte read/write causes many system calls; use bulk reads into a buffer to reduce overhead and improve throughput.. In practical terms, what happens when you copy one byte at a time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Buffering stores data in memory temporarily so that your program can read and write in larger blocks instead of making many small system calls. When you wrap a FileInputStream with a BufferedInputStream, the wrapper performs an underlying read once to fill its internal buffer and then serves subsequent byte requests from memory. This reduces context switches and the number of expensive disk reads. A concrete example: a 4KB buffer causes roughly one system call per 4KB of file data, versus one per byte without buffering. BufferedOutputStream behaves similarly on writes: it collects bytes into an internal buffer and writes them out in larger chunks. A common misconception is that buffering only reduces latency; in fact, it primarily increases throughput by reducing syscall overhead. Another developer pitfall is choosing an extremely large buffer; while bigger buffers reduce syscalls further, they also use more memory and can yield diminishing returns. Start with 4KB to 8KB, measure performance, and adjust based on empirical results. The main takeaway: buffering moves work from slow input and output to fast memory operations. Try-with-resources ensures streams are closed automatically when a block finishes or when an exception is thrown. For file streams, this prevents file descriptors being leaked, which could otherwise exhaust system resources in long-running processes. The pattern is simple: declare your streams in the try(...) header and omit explicit close calls. Under the hood, the JVM calls close on each AutoCloseable in reverse order, which also flushes BufferedOutputStream. Avoid the mistake of catching exceptions and swallowing them without ensuring closure. A concrete example: if a copy operation throws an IOException while writing, try-with-resources still closes the streams and flushes buffered output on close, reducing the risk of truncated files. If you need to guarantee data reaches disk immediately before continuing, call flush explicitly; close will usually flush, but flush before critical points is safer. Overall, prefer try-with-resources for clarity and resource safety in all stream-based input and output.
